rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act (criminal-history screening limits)
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not put criminal-record questions on an application. They also may not make any oral or written inquiry about criminal records before a conditional offer. Two exceptions apply: methamphetamine manufacture on federally assisted premises, and lifetime sex-offender registration. At no point may a provider evaluate any of these records: arrests or charges without conviction, expunged convictions, pardoned convictions, vacated or nullified convictions, juvenile adjudications, or sealed records. After a conditional offer, a provider may consider only two kinds of records. The first is convictions for murder, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, arson, human trafficking, the listed sexual offenses, or any crime resulting in lifetime registration. The second is indictable offenses within lookback periods: 6 years for first degree, 4 years for second or third degree, and 1 year for fourth degree. A conditional offer may be withdrawn only if the provider finds, by a preponderance of the evidence, that withdrawal is necessary to a substantial, legitimate and nondiscriminatory interest. That finding must follow an individualized assessment of listed factors. Withdrawal requires written notice giving specific reasons and an opportunity to appeal. The applicant may request the information relied on within 30 days, and the provider must supply it free within 10 days. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is reviewed and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracies or rehabilitation. Drug and alcohol tests, and requests for consent to obtain drug-treatment information, are prohibited. Enforcement is by complaint to the Division on Civil Rights only, not in court. The Division offers a 14-day mediation window. Penalties are up to $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000 depending on prior violations. The director may also order the application fee returned and up to $1,000 paid to the applicant.
rules.key_value: Post-offer lookback 6 / 4 / 1 years by offense degree; records request within 30 days, free response within 10 days; penalties up to $1,000 / $5,000 / $10,000

rules.title: Residential rental application fee cap ($50, CPI-adjusted)
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee above $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes. Penalties are up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second and $1,000 for each later offense. They are enforced in summary proceedings in the Special Civil Part on complaint of the Director of Consumer Affairs or the Attorney General. The amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant. Beginning January 1 of the year after enactment, the Director adjusts the cap annually by the CPI (NY-Northern NJ-Long Island, All Items), only when the change is greater than zero, and publishes it online. The Director must adopt rules, including a mechanism for reporting violations.

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement: A security deposit may not exceed 1.5 times one month's rent, and that limit includes any pet deposit and any prepaid rent held as security, such as last month's rent. At lease inception the landlord may collect at most 2.5 times the monthly rent, counting the deposit and first month's rent. Yearly increases may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. The deposit is held in trust, may not be commingled, and must be kept in an interest-bearing account at an insured New Jersey institution. Landlords holding deposits for 10 or more units may instead use an insured New Jersey money market fund. Interest belongs to the tenant. Within 30 days of receipt, the landlord must give written notice of the institution, amount, account type and interest rate. If notice or interest is not provided, the tenant may apply the deposit plus 7% annual interest to rent. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit plus interest, less itemized deductions sent by personal delivery or registered or certified mail. The deadline is 5 business days if the tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation. It is 15 business days after a Safe Housing Act termination. A tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld, plus costs and attorney's fees.

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act (good cause eviction)
rules.requirement:
A residential landlord may not evict or refuse to renew a lease, written or oral, without good cause. The statutory causes are:
- nonpayment of rent
- disorderly conduct
- willful or grossly negligent damage
- substantial breach of rules or lease covenants after a Notice to Cease
- nonpayment of a rent increase that is not unconscionable
- health and safety or illegal-occupancy removal
- permanent retirement from residential use
- refusal of reasonable lease changes
- habitual late payment
- condominium, cooperative or fee-simple conversion
- post-conversion owner or buyer occupancy
- end of employment-based tenancy
- certain drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking findings

A written Notice to Quit is required for every cause except nonpayment. The notice period depends on the cause: 3 days, 1 month, 2 months, 3 months, 18 months or 3 years. Only a court judgment and warrant for removal can remove a tenant, and self-help eviction is illegal. Tenants removed for illegal occupancy get relocation assistance of 6 times the monthly rent. Misuse after an owner-occupancy eviction exposes the landlord to treble damages. Residential reuse within 5 years of a retirement or demolition eviction carries treble damages and a civil penalty of up to $10,000. Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings may be evicted only for a narrower list of causes, including holdover after lease expiry. Holdover requires 3 months' notice for at-will or year-to-year tenancies and 1 month for month-to-month tenancies. Rooming and boarding houses follow the same causes and must give 3 working days' notice to the County Welfare Board.
rules.key_value: Notice to Quit: 3 days (disorderly, damage, employment, criminal causes); 1 month (rules/lease breach, rent increase, lease changes, late payment); 2 months (post-conversion occupancy); 3 months (health/safety); 18 months (retirement); 3 years (conversion); relocation 6x monthly rent for illegal occupancy

rules.title: Foreclosure tenant protections and notices (Foreclosure Fairness Act)
rules.requirement: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction. A buyer who wants to occupy a foreclosed property as a primary residence must give a 90-day notice to quit. A tenant whose lease runs longer cannot be evicted until the lease expires. Anyone acquiring a foreclosed property with rental units must notify tenants in English and Spanish within 10 business days of the sale that ownership has changed and they need not move. In buildings with more than 10 units, the notice is posted in a prominent location instead. Foreclosing creditors must give the court-rule notice of tenant rights. A monetary offer to induce a tenant to leave must come with a separate notice and a five-day review period, and pressure tactics are prohibited.

coverage.summary: Applies to residential rental units in foreclosed properties. Month-to-month tenants and owner-occupied two- and three-family units are not exempt from the 90-day notice.

rules.effective_date_note: The guide states no effective date.

rules.title: Reprisal protections for tenants
rules.requirement:
A landlord may not retaliate by eviction, by substantially altering the lease or its terms, or by refusing to renew when a tenant exercises protected rights. Protected rights are:
- enforcing rights under the lease or law
- making a good-faith complaint to a government authority, after first notifying the landlord in writing and allowing reasonable time to fix the problem
- organizing or joining a lawful tenant organization
- refusing lease changes made in retaliation

The tenant may sue for damages.

rules.title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (conversion protected tenancy)
rules.requirement: Eligible tenants in a building being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership may obtain protected tenancy. Eligibility requires age 62 or older before the conversion recording date, permanent disability, or a service-connected disability of 60% or more for an honorably discharged veteran. The tenant must also have lived in the building at least one year before the conversion recording date. Protected tenants are shielded from eviction for 40 years if family income is no more than three times the county average per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater. The landlord or converter must notify tenants of the right to apply. Applications are generally due within 60 days.

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income and other protected characteristics
rules.requirement: The LAD prohibits housing discrimination based on source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment. It also bars discrimination based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital, civil union or domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, disability and nationality. For example, a landlord cannot deny a Section 8 voucher holder an apartment based solely on that source of income. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income or poor credit history. Complaints may be filed free with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or in Superior Court within two years. Fines are up to $10,000 for a first offense.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement:
Each of the following is unlawful and a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act:
- a rental property owner or its agent paying for, subscribing to or contracting for the services of a coordinator
- a coordinator facilitating an agreement among owners that restricts competition, including by performing a coordinating function
- two or more persons engaging in or facilitating parallel pricing coordination
- any person performing a coordinating function

A coordinating function is algorithmic or automated rent, lease-term or occupancy setting or recommending that uses nonpublic, competitively sensitive information of other owners, or that uses a common algorithm for two or more owners. Antitrust Act remedies (C.56:9-6 to 9-17) apply. The Attorney General must set up a complaint location and may adopt rules. Municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.
rules.key_value: Violations are New Jersey Antitrust Act violations; effective July 1, 2027; conflicting municipal ordinances prohibited

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Any rental property owner owning one or more rental residential dwelling units. Controlled entities count as a single owner.
coverage.summary: Covers residential dwelling units used as primary residences in New Jersey (houses, apartments, accessory units). Inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care and detention or correctional facilities are excluded.
coverage.other_conditions: Not a coordinating function: research or testing not used to set rents; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage listing databases that do not set or recommend rents; government affordability controls. Not an algorithmic device: non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis; databases that only query unprocessed data.

rules.exemptions: Research and testing uses; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage databases; government affordability controls; non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis; query-only databases.

rules.conflict_note: Section 6(b) bars municipal ordinances that conflict with the act. Once the act takes effect on July 1, 2027, it may preempt the Jersey City (Code § 218-12) and Hoboken (Code § 158-2) algorithmic rent-setting ordinances, at least where they differ. For example, Jersey City exempts an owner's coordination across its own properties, while the act's coordinating function reaches owners acting for their own benefit. It exempts newly constructed multiple dwellings from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. It caps no rents itself, so it belongs in the new_construction_exemption coverage of municipal rent control records (e.g., Jersey City ch. 260), not in a state record.
